question.knowledge_point: Finding the Velocity of a Particle Whose Acceleration Is Not a Polynomial
question.problem: A particle moves along a straight line relative to a fixed origin $O$ with acceleration, measured in $\text{m}/{\text{s}}^{2},$ given by the function $a(t)=-6{e}^{-2t}$, where $t$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=2\,\text{m}/\text{s}$ when $t=0\,\text{s}$, find the velocity (in $\text{m/s}$)  of the particle at time $t.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find $v(t)$ by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (-6{e}^{-2t})\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6(-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{-2t})+C \\  & =3{e}^{-2t}+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C$, we use the fact that $v(0)=2.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}2 & =3{e}^{0}+C \\ 2 & =3+C \\ C & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the velocity $v$ of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=3{e}^{-2t}-1.$

question.knowledge_point: Creating an Integral Expression For the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/3a760f55b6437a39010e4d1a00bdb5fb5390d848dd74347e7736e2ac49cd562b.png)

Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta )$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}$ (shown in blue in the diagram above)?
question.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ),$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ).
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}+(12\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\theta ))^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+144{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta ))}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(4\theta )+16{cos}^{2}⁡(4\theta )}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Finding the Arc Length of a Polar Curve
question.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067289/assets/3387790df770ac8645058c6f460b1f1285629d18d765668e362a8070ae4035ed.png)

Find the arc length of the polar curve $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ for $0\le \theta \le \pi $ (shown in blue in the diagram above).

*Hint: You may wish to use the following identity: $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}.$*
question.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{(2+2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{8+8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{8}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Now, we recall the identity for $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2}):$

$$
\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{x}{2})=\sqrt{\frac{1+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}
$$

Therefore, using $x=\theta $ in the previous identity, the integral can be written as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot {\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={4\cdot 2(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =8(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =8.\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the Arc Length of a Polar Curve

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
question.problem: Given that $u=1+{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to $\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $u=1+{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x\,⟹\,x\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\text{d}u.
$$

We also note that
${x}^{2}=u-1$

Now we can rewrite the integral in terms of $u:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{x}^{3}\,\text{d}x}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{1+{x}^{2}}}\cdot {x}^{2}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{u}}\cdot (u-1)\cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int ({u}^{1/2}-{u}^{-1/2})\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating Indefinite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution

question.knowledge_point: Calculating Definite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution
question.problem: Given that $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, which integral is equivalent to ${\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $u=3-2{x}^{2}$, then we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=-4x\,⟹\,-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}=x\text{d}x.
$$

We also note that ${x}^{2}=\frac{1}{2}(3-u).$ 

Computing our limits of integration, we get

| **$x$** | $-1$ | $0$ |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **$u$** | $1$ | $3$ |

We can now solve the integral using our new variable $u,$ remembering to use the new limits of integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{3}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{x}^{2}\sqrt{3-2{x}^{2}}\cdot x\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{2}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\cdot (-\frac{\text{d}u}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{1}^{3}(3-u)\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Calculating Definite Integrals of Algebraic Functions Using Substitution

question.knowledge_point: Using the Trapezoidal Rule: Word Problem
question.problem:
The following table shows the number of customers per minute, $c(t),$ that arrive at a shop counter over a period of $120$ minutes.

| $t\,(\text{minutes})$ | $0$ | $30$ | $80$ | $120$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $c(t)\,(\text{customers/minute})$ | $10$ | $8$ | $6$ | $12$ |

Use the trapezoidal rule with the partition

$$
[0,30]\cup [30,80]\cup [80,120],
$$

to approximate the total number of customers served in two hours.
question.worked_solution:
In this context, we have $3$ trapezoids, and the area $A$ under the curve $y=c(t)$ represents the total number of customers served in $2$ hours.

Using the trapezoidal rule, we estimate the area as follows:

$$
A≈\frac{c(0)+c(30)}{2}\cdot Δ{t}_{1}+\frac{c(30)+c(80)}{2}\cdot Δ{t}_{2}+\frac{c(80)+c(120)}{2}\cdot Δ{t}_{3}
$$

Substituting the appropriate numbers into the above expression gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ≈\frac{10+8}{2}\cdot (30-0)+\frac{8+6}{2}\cdot (80-30)+\frac{6+12}{2}\cdot (120-80) \\  & =9\cdot 30+7\cdot 50+9\cdot 40 \\  & =980\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the total number of customers serve approximately is $980$ in $2$ hours.

question.knowledge_point: Identifying the Linear Transformation Represented by a Matrix
question.problem: Which of the following represents a reflection across the $x$-axis?
question.worked_solution:
The correct answer is $T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].$ Indeed, consider the standard basis $\{i,j\}$ of the Euclidean plane ${R}^{2}$ and the unit square spanned by the vectors, as shown below.

Now, we can find the images of $\{i,j\}$ under $T$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{i}^{′} & =T(i)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=i \\ {j}^{′} & =T(j)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=-j\end{aligned}

question.knowledge_point: Optimizing the Area of a Rectangle
question.problem: A gardener wants to fence a rectangular flowerbed with $15$ meters of fencing. To two decimal places, what is the largest area that he can make with the fencing?
question.worked_solution:
**Step 1**: Let us call $x$ and $y$ the dimensions of the rectangle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14067869/assets/bebb7c4ca5e38d75136146f6e4547b0e72d529ce24453a3d0212bca1ffbfe4c0.png)

**Step 2**: We need to find the values of $x$ and $y$ such as the area

$$
A=xy
$$

is the greatest possible value.

**Step 3**: This is subject to the constraint that the perimeter is $15.$ This gives the equation

$$
2x+2y=15.
$$

**Step 4**: We make one of the variables the subject in the constraint equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+2y & =15 \\ y & =\frac{15}{2}-x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $y=\frac{15}{2}-x$ in the expression $A=xy$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =x(\frac{15}{2}-x) \\ A & =\frac{15}{2}x-{x}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 5**: We solve the equation ${A}^{′}(x)=0.$ Taking the derivative, we have

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=\frac{15}{2}-2x,
$$

and solving for the stationary points, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ \frac{15}{2}-2x & =0 \\ 2x & =\frac{15}{2} \\ x & =\frac{15}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 6**: We confirm that $x=\frac{15}{4}$ is a maximum using the second derivative test. The second derivative is

$$
{A}^{″}(x)=-2\,⟹\,{A}^{″}(\frac{15}{4})=-2<0.
$$

Since ${A}^{″}(\frac{15}{4})$ is negative, we conclude that $x=\frac{15}{4}$ is indeed a maximum of $A(x).$

Finally, when $x=\frac{15}{4}$, we have 

$$
y=\frac{15}{2}-\frac{15}{4}=\frac{15}{4}.
$$

Therefore, the dimensions of the rectangle with the largest area are $x=\frac{15}{4}$ and $y=\frac{15}{4},$ and we conclude that

$$
A=xy=\frac{15}{4}\cdot \frac{15}{4}≈14.06
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

provenance.kp_title: Optimizing the Area of a Rectangle

question.knowledge_point: Rewriting One of the Limits of an Improper Integral
question.problem:
Which of the following is equivalent to 
${\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{\text{d}x}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}?$
question.worked_solution:
This is an improper integral of the second kind because the function under the integral is unbounded as we approach the *upper* integration limit from any point that lies in the interval $x\in (-6,-3):$

$$
f(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\to \infty \,\text{as}\,x\to (-3)^{-}
$$

We can attempt to evaluate this integral by integrating $f(x)$ over the interval $x\in [-6,b]$ and taking the limit as $b\to (-3)^{-}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-6}^{-3}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{b\to (-3)^{-}}({\int }_{-6}^{b}\frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-9}}\,\text{d}x)\end{aligned}
$$

provenance.kp_title: Rewriting One of the Limits of an Improper Integral

question.knowledge_point: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value
question.problem:
What is the first term that is less than $0.001$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
64,\,48,\,36,\,27,\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=64$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{48}{64}=\frac{3}{4}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be less than $0.001.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & <0.001 \\ 64{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <0.001 \\ {(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\frac{0.001}{64} \\ \operatorname{log}⁡{(\frac{3}{4})}^{n-1} & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ (n-1)\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4}) & <\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016) \\ n-1 & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})} \\ n & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we reversed the inequality sign when divided by $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ because $\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})$ is a negative number. 

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(0.000\,016)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(\frac{3}{4})}+1≈39.386
$$

Therefore, the $40$th term is the first term of the sequence that is less than $0.001.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding the First Term Smaller Than a Given Value

question.knowledge_point: Finding a Variable Point Closest to a Fixed Point
question.problem: If the distance between the points $(3a-4,a+2)$ and $(-2,6)$ is minimized, then $a=$
question.worked_solution:
First, let's compute the *squared* distance $S(a)$ between the two points. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}S(a) & ={(3a-4-(-2))}^{2}+{(a+2-6)}^{2} \\  & =(3a-2)^{2}+(a-4)^{2} \\  & =9{a}^{2}-12a+4+{a}^{2}-8a+16 \\  & =10{a}^{2}-20a+20.\end{aligned}
$$

Since we want to minimize $S,$ we compute the derivative ${S}^{′}(a).$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(a) & =20a-20.\end{aligned}
$$

The stationary points of $S(a)$ are the points where the derivative ${S}^{′}(a)=0.$ Solving this equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}^{′}(a) & =0 \\ 20a-20 & =0 \\ a & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can see that ${S}^{″}(1)=20>0.$ Therefore, the squared distance (and therefore the actual distance) reaches a minimum when $b=1.$

provenance.kp_title: Finding a Variable Point Closest to a Fixed Point
